title: Dr. Raj Panjabi at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Dr. Raj Panjabi —Former White House Senior Director, Senior Partner at Flagship Pioneering, and Associate Physician at Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School—for a discussion of his new book, Safer: A Playbook—Turning Fear into Action and Crisis into Community. About Safer The essential guide for navigating crisis and uncertainty from the acclaimed physician who led the White House response to the world’s most dangerous health emergencies. When crisis hits—a sudden illness, a global disruption, or a career upheaval—our instinct is to retreat. Yet decades of research prove that our greatest protection isn’t isolation, it’s connection. From high-stakes decisions in the White House Situation Room and hospital emergency room to dramatic shocks of violence and illness his family struggled with in their own living room, Dr. Raj Panjabi has navigated humanity’s most precarious moments. Now, he translates hard-earned wisdom into a step-by-step roadmap. Through gripping storytelling and cutting-edge science, Safer reveals the eight practical “plays” to protect what matters most at home and work. You will learn how to: Navigate Fear and Denial: Use Situation Room insights to take decisive action without falling into paralysis. Cut Through the Noise: Use science to assess your risk and protect those you love amidst the flood of misinformation. Build Trust in Divided Times: Move from isolation to connection and find common ground. Gain Control Despite Chaos: Adapt to change and transform vulnerability into your greatest strength. In an era of uncertainty, you don’t have to live in fear. You just need a better playbook. Safer gives us the tools for emerging from any crisis more connected than ever before.

Edward Steed continues his winning streak as the most exciting cartoonist in The New Yorker’s pages in the 21st century. title: Stems & Sips: Sake & Ikebana
description: Saturday, October 31, 6:30-8:00pm EST Find your flow, one branch and one pour at a time. True harmony happens when you strip things down to their absolute essence. In Japan, this philosophy connects two beautiful crafts: Ikebana (minimalist floral arrangement) and Sake (the refined art of brewing). Join us for Stems & Sips, a relaxed, hands-on evening designed for beginners. No complex jargon, no overwhelming flower bundles—just clean flavors, striking lines, and a healthy dose of fun. What to Expect Sake Demystified: Discover the stunning versatility of premium sake. You’ll taste a curated flight—ranging from bright and fruity to crisp and earthy—while learning the basics of how it’s made and served. The Living Sculpture: Dive into Ikebana, the traditional art of flower arrangement. Unlike dense Western bouquets, Ikebana focuses on negative space, asymmetry, and making a few thoughtful stems speak volumes. Guided Creation: We will walk you through the core principles of line, depth, and form. Step-by-step, you’ll learn how to position branches and blossoms to mimic the grace of nature. No experience required. We provide the tools, the knowledge, and the liquid inspiration. You’ll leave with a gorgeous centerpiece, a newfound appreciation for Japanese craft, and a serious sense of zen. Cost: $150 Location: Commonwealth Wine School, Cambridge, MA Instructor: Marina Giordano ENROLL HERE

Taste different wines alongside a selection of Halloween chocolates and candies, compare the combinations for yourself, and learn a few simple principles you can use at home long after Halloween is over. As always at Bonde, expect serious wine without the seriousness: an intimate group, plenty of tasting and conversation, and a relaxed, unpretentious atmosphere where experimentation is encouraged, and questions are always welcome. title: The Commute
description: The Commute SHOW DESCRIPTION: Four strangers are trapped in a tunnel during a sudden stop on the Red Line. As tension builds, they are forced to confront each other-and themselves. The Commute is a dark, thought provoking new comedy by Karin Anell, exploring human behavior under pressure. Who are we really, behind our masks? The evening show will be followed by an interactive talk-back and panel discussing the evolving role of technology in our lives. ARTIST STATEMENT: “I love listening to people’s life stories. My scripts are often based on individuals’ lived experiences and I believe in theatre as a powerful vehicle to bring these engaging narratives to life. Theatre can bring people together to start important conversations, and I don’t mean discussions around who was the better actor, or whether the third act was too long. I want people to leave the theatre and spend the next couple of hours discussing what they saw. How did this piece make them feel? What are they thinking right now? Did this play open their eyes to something new; see the world, and themselves, in a different light? I like to include interactive sessions with a subject matter expert(s) after performances. I moderate these sessions, inviting the audience to participate and ask questions about what they saw. Themes I have brought to life include a mother’s guilt, body image, and our biggest fears. It does not take a million-dollar production that runs for 3 hours to engage an audience and stimulate an interesting debate. I believe in: Simplicity and adaptability-use modern technology to make theatre more engaging and entertaining Short plays that pack a punch, using local talent Community-based theatre accessible to all” — Karin Anell SOCIAL MEDIAS: Facebook: tcsquaredthea tre / Instagram: @tc2theatre Timeline: EARLY SHOW: DOORS: 1:15 PM SHOW: 2:00 PM LATE SHOW (With Panel!): DOORS: 5:15 PM SHOW: 6:00 PM Age Limit: This event is All Ages ID: Valid ID required for Alcohol Consumption Limited Late

title: Monday Moments for Friends, Fellows, and Partners
description: We invite Friends, Fellows, and Partners of the museums to explore two fascinating exhibitions at their own pace through a self-guided visit: On Location: Drawing the Outdoors (September 18, 2026–January 17, 2027) and The Way We Never Were: The American Professional Photographers Collection (August 29, 2026–May 9, 2027). In the exhibition On Location: Drawing the Outdoors, discover how an intimate relationship with nature shaped the artistic vision of 19th-century European artists. Featuring approximately 140 sketches, watercolors, and pastels by artists including J. M. W. Turner, Berthe Morisot, Paul Cézanne, and Vincent van Gogh, the exhibition is organized as a series of thematic journeys through the landscape and explores changing ideas about nature, environmental awareness, and artistic identity. It invites visitors to reflect on why these artists’ experiences of the outdoors continue to resonate today. The Way We Never Were explores how professional photography helped shape Americans’ understanding of life after World War II. Drawn from the Harvard Art Museums’ American Professional Photographers Collection, the exhibition features commissioned photographs of weddings, schools, businesses, and other everyday moments that presented an idealized vision of postwar America. These images not only documented the era but also influenced cultural memory by highlighting certain experiences while leaving others out. Through themes of prosperity, suburbia, conformity, and the struggle for equal rights, the exhibition encourages visitors to reconsider the story these photographs tell about the American past. This special preview is our way of thanking you for your support and dedication to the Harvard Art Museums. To become a Friend, Fellow, or Partner, please visit our Support page. Join today to take advantage of this exclusive opportunity. Funding for On Location: Drawing the Outdoors and related programming was provided by the Stanley H. Durwood Foundation Support Fun

title: Rachel Dorothy Tanur Memorial Lecture: Pneuhaus “Building with Air”
description: Pneuhaus began by blowing bubbles: a joint thesis project built around a fascination with inflatables and what could be made of them at a craft level. This talk traces how that early curiosity grew into a full-fledged art, design, and fabrication studio. Working hands-on with materials and techniques eventually shaped an unusual business model, closer to a traveling circus than a design studio, where work packs down small, travels light, and can go up almost anywhere in the world. August Lehrecke, Pneuhaus co-founder, will cover how making and installing their work built the studio Pneuhaus runs today, and how commissioned projects sharpen the skills and tools they carry back into the creative practice. Underneath it all is a fascination with how much a shift in air pressure can change: soft turns rigid, a surface lets light through or blocks it out, or a structure deforms underfoot. Lehrecke will discuss various studio projects and the areas the studio is currently exploring.

title: Artist Talk: Enzo Camacho and Ami Lien
description: The 2026 Nancy Stephenson Nichols Memorial Lecture Join visual artists and Harvard alumni Enzo Camacho (A.B. ’07) and Ami Lien (A.B. ’09) as they share insights and developments into their practice as artistic collaborators. Working between New York, Berlin, and Manila, Camacho and Lien develop research-based, site-specific, and documentary projects to examine histories of labor, land, and resistance in the Philippines. Their research on the enduring influence of Alfonso Ossorio’s mural commission at the Chapel of St. Joseph the Worker on Negros Island has led them to investigate the sugar plantation landscape that grounds this historic site-specific artwork. In their ongoing engagement with Negros Island, the artists focus on the defiant forms of culture-making that emerge out of and in opposition to plantation violence. This program is offered in conjunction with Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage (October 23, 2026–April 11, 2027) in Gallery 1120 at the Harvard Art Museums and Knowledge Is Myth: Chimeric Continuities (October 1–December 13, 2026) at the Carpenter Center for Visual Arts. This event is part of In Conversation, a series of evening programs that feature local and international curators, artists, scholars, and more. Running from September through April, these events highlight our temporary exhibitions, permanent collections, and a range of creative voices.

title: Materials Lab Workshop: Making an Impression
description: Join assistant paper conservator Abby Schleicher and research curator Francesca Bewer for a workshop focused on art and science. You’ll discover how different printmaking techniques record both intentional design and the physical traces of making. Through hands-on experimentation using a variety of tools, pressures, inks, and papers, you’ll see how each technical choice leaves distinct traces—and why no two impressions are ever truly identical. We’ll look at a selection of prints under magnification and specialized conservation lighting to “read” their toolmarks, plate wear, inking, and condition. Linking studio experiments with close looking from a conservation perspective, this workshop will give you a concrete framework for identifying print processes and a richer appreciation of the material complexity of printed images. This workshop is one of four offered this fall that explore different media through the lens of art and science. Take one or take them all! The four workshops are: Saturday, September 19: Landscape Drawing with Optical Devices Wednesday, October 7: Color Alchemy—Pigments and DIY Paint Friday, November 6: Making an Impression Friday, November 20: Casting Connections—Molds, Replicas, and Questions of Authorship

title: Jaqueline Tyrwhitt Urban Design Lecture: Dana Cuff “Coming Home: Crisis, Fire, and Recovery”
description: Dr. Dana Cuff, an educator, scholar, designer, and activist who explores how design can contribute to building more just and equitable cities, work on rebuilding after the 2025 Eaton Fire in Altadena and the housing crisis in Los Angeles. In 2006, Cuff founded cityLAB, a research and design center that initiates experimental projects to explore more equitable metropolitan possibilities. Starting in 2019, cityLAB expanded its social and political engagement by creating long term partnerships with community organizations in the region, first in the Westlake/MacArthur Park neighborhood of Los Angeles, and after the devastating fires of 2025, in Altadena. cityLAB has developed sustainable, high-performance, low-cost housing prototypes for infill sites ranging from backyards to schoolyards. Cuff will address the lab’s projects with a focus on its community-led, post-fire initiatives. Dr. Dana Cuff, a leader in urban innovation, is a Distinguished Professor at UCLA who engages spatial justice and cultural studies of architecture as a teacher, scholar, practitioner, and activist. In 2017, after a decade of research that included a full-scale demonstration house built on the UCLA campus, Cuff co-authored the first of her several pieces of California State legislation, opening 8.1M single-family lots for secondary rental units. In 2024, she launched “Small Lots, Big Impacts,” a design-development initiative to build a new generation of dense, compact starter homes on publicly-held land. Cuff has authored numerous books, includingArchitectures of Spatial Justice(MIT Press, 2023),Urban Humanities: New Practices for Reimagining the City(MIT Press, 2020),Architects’ People(with W.R. Ellis; 1989), andArchitecture: The Story of Practice(1989).

title: Infrastructure in a Time of Flux: Methods, Conditions, and Situations Symposium
description: Infrastructure in a Time of Flux: Methods, Conditions, and Situations, an exhibition curated by Rahul Mehrotra and Dan Borelli, examines how architecture, engineering, urban design, and planning respond to a world increasingly defined by environmental disruption, political instability, technological transformation, migration, and rapidly changing patterns of habitation. This symposium brings together designers, architects, humanitarian workers, and historians to reflect on the exhibition’s three themes and a case study: Methods:This panel explores historic and contemporary approaches to lightweight construction: suspended, pneumatic, tensile, tensegrity, deployable, gridshell, folded, scaffolding, and spaceframe systems. Developed across different periods and disciplines, these methods use tension, air pressure, geometry, movement, modularity, and coordinated assemblies to create expansive spaces with relatively little material.Conditions:This panel brings together urbanists, economists, and political scientists to discuss the forces that continually reshape human settlements. These forces operate beyond the scale of individual buildings, transforming landscapes, redistributing resources, influencing migration, and determining where and how communities can live.Situations:Designers and researchers present contemporary examples and speculative proposals for structures that meet immediate human needs. title: Materials Lab Workshop: Casting Connections—Molds, Replicas, and Questions of Authorship
description: Join research curator Francesca Bewer for a workshop focused on art and science. We’ll explore the intimate connections between models, molds, and casts; how molds and casts have been used to produce, replicate, and preserve three-dimensional objects; and what these objects can teach us about skill, technology, and value. Working with clay, plaster, wax, alginate, and silicone putty, we’ll experiment with different processes of molding and casting. Along the way, you’ll be introduced to the scientific tools used to investigate and identify the traces of process and change. Through discussion and comparison with historical plaster casts, wax models, and other surrogates in the Harvard Art Museums collections, we’ll ask when a copy might be considered “fake,” “genuine,” or something in between, and how replicas support research, teaching, and conservation in museums today. This workshop is one of four offered this fall that explore different media through the lens of art and science. Take one or take them all! The four workshops are: Saturday, September 19: Landscape Drawing with Optical Devices Wednesday, October 7: Color Alchemy—Pigments and DIY Paint Friday, November 6: Making an Impression Friday, November 20: Casting Connections—Molds, Replicas, and Questions of Authorship

title: Carl M. Sapers Ethics in Practice Lecture: Sylvia Lavin “Architecture After Fire”
description: This lecture, “Architecture After Fire,” argues that the rise of American architectural modernism was inseparable from the forest, not because of the use of timber, but because of modernism’s reliance on arboreal media—employing trees as information and communication systems and as metaphors. Tracking the white pine through deforestation, wildfire, and the formation of the Chicago school, this paper explores the series of substitutions, each triggered by fire, that converted environmental catastrophe into aesthetic doctrine and designated these operations as the primary function of modern architecture, artistically considered.

While participants come from a range of lived experiences—including adoption, foster care, donor conception, and unexpected family discoveries—the lineup reflects those who have chosen to step forward and share their stories this year. Together, these voices create a collective portrait of what it means to grow up without full access to one’s origins, and the ongoing search for connection, meaning, and belonging. Kristal Parke is a talented filmmaker, producer, speaker and podcaster whose work explores identity, belonging, and resilience. A transracial adoptee from a closed adoption, her personal journey fuels her storytelling with authenticity, compassion, and truth. She creates space for unheard voices, shaping narratives that educate, challenge, inspire and heal. Conceived by Uschenko after cutting his teeth as a touring multi-instrumentalist, the project was brought to life in an abandoned farmhouse in Diamond City, Alberta. There, for two months, he would make the self-released, self-titled debut album which was produced and dubbed directly to custom-made cassette tapes. The music has always been beautifully inhospitable, earned only by those curious enough to seek it out. — Dine Alone Records Presented by Get To The Gig & MassConcerts Ages: Show age differs by the day. title: John Constable and the Outdoors: Writing about Drawing
description: In conjunction with the exhibition On Location: Drawing the Outdoors, author and scholar Susan Owens will share John Constable’s sketches, paintings, diaries, and letters to trace the creative process of a painter in love with nature. In conversation with curator Joachim Homann, she will discuss sketching outside, looking, and writing. This lecture will be recorded and made available for online viewing; check back shortly after the event for the link to view the recording. On Location: Drawing the Outdoors features drawings by J. M. W. Turner, John Constable, Gustave Courbet, Edouard Manet, Berthe Morisot, Paul Cézanne, and Vincent van Gogh, among many others. The exhibition is on view from September 18, 2026 to January 17, 2027. This event is part of In Conversation, a series of evening programs that feature local and international curators, artists, scholars, and more. Running from September through April, these events highlight our temporary exhibitions, permanent collections, and a range of creative voices. title: Harvard Art Museums at Night
description: Make your holiday season more festive at the Harvard Art Museums! Join us for an evening of art, fun, food, and more! Gather with friends and mingle inside our spectacular Italian-inspired courtyard, evoking the energy of a bustling town piazza. DJ C-Zone will set the mood with smooth, curated sounds as you chat, snack, sip, and catch up over bites and drinks available for purchase from local vendors. Get a head start on your holiday shopping by taking advantage of a 10% discount at the museum shop. Drop in on a Spotlight Tour, then make art in the Materials Lab. You can also enter to win an original work from the Harvard Ceramics Program! The galleries are yours to explore, with more than 50 spaces filled with world-class art. There are prizes to be won, friends to be made, and favorite artworks to be found! Don’t forget to check out our current exhibitions. Harvard Art Museums at Night takes place the last Thursday of every month (holidays permitting), from 5 to 9pm. Each night features a new mix of local talent and community partners to make this a festive occasion for all. WBUR is the media partner for Harvard Art Museums at Night. This event is part of ArtsThursdays, a university-wide initiative supported by Harvard University Committee on the Arts (HUCA).

title: The Material Culture of Islamic Calligraphy
description: The 2026 Norma Jean Calderwood Lecture Calligraphy is the most recognizable of Islamic arts, and it is often seen in its finished form—an inscription written on paper; carved in stone, wood, or ivory; cast in metal; or woven into fabric. Yet calligraphy always begins as a trace left by a pen, a practice sustained by a rich material culture. Cultural historian İrvin Cemil Schick looks at the wide array of tools used in the artistic practice of Islamic calligraphy, such as reed pens, penknives, cutting boards, inks, inkwells, papers, and scissors. Speaker: İrvin Cemil Schick, Cultural historian İrvin Cemil Schick is a cultural and intellectual historian specializing in the Ottoman Empire. He holds Ph.D.s from MIT and the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales, in Paris, and has taught at Harvard University, MIT, and Istanbul Şehir University. He has also held guest positions at Boston University, Sabancı University, Boğaziçi University, and the University of Massachusetts, Amherst. His principal research interests include the Islamic arts of the book, particularly calligraphy, illumination, and marbling; gender, sexuality, spatiality, and the body in Islam; animals and the environment in Islam; and occult practices in Islam. This event is part of In Conversation, a series of evening programs that feature local and international curators, artists, scholars, and more. Running from September through April, these events highlight our temporary exhibitions, permanent collections, and a range of creative voices.

title: Gallery Talk: Crafting Perfect Portraits with Photographic Proof Prints
description: Join Madison Brown, co-curator of The Way We Never Were: The American Professional Photographers Collection (August 29, 2026–May 9, 2027), for a discussion about the role of proof prints in the craft of producing polished studio portraits. Rather than capturing a single decisive moment behind the camera, the finished portrait is a result of a multi-step process. The proof prints are used by professional photographers to chart plans for retouching portraits, and photographers’ handwritten notations invite us to explore the extensive and collaborative work behind the sleek finished products. Led by: Madison Brown, Smithsonian Institution Postdoctoral Fellow, National Museum of American History, and former John R. and Barbara Robinson Family Curatorial Fellow in Photography, Division of Modern and Contemporary Art, Harvard Art Museums Funding for the exhibition and related programming was provided by the John R. and Barbara Robinson Family Fund for Photography and the M.
